https://www.politico.eu/article/france-t.text: PARIS — Is France ready for a crisis that plunges it into darkness? The French government is planning to find out. The government is looking to organize a tabletop simulation of a sudden, nationwide power outage in the second half of 2027, according to four people with direct knowledge of the exercise, who were granted anonymity to discuss plans that have not been publicly announced. The exercise will involve the French electricity grid operators Enedis and RTE as well as several government departments and ministries and the French military administration. Advertisement Advertisement Its purpose will be to determine how the country would respond to a paralyzing electricity outage of the kind that hit Spain and Portugal in April 2025, or a major cyberattack targeting the power grid as Poland experienced last year — an act of sabotage Brussels has attributed to Russian intelligence services. The simulation will test “the country's ability to respond," said one person familiar with preparations for the exercise, adding that it is intended to assess the time needed to restore power and the country’s ability to ensure the continuity of essential services. The exercise was formally confirmed during an interministerial committee on national resilience on July 8. A detailed announcement should come before the end of the year. The meeting notes outline other priorities, such as making sure the French state maintains access to goods considered "essential to ensuring the continuity of the state and the protection of the population." These include “emergency blankets, generators, medicines, telecommunications equipment, equipment for law enforcement, as well as rare and critical raw materials.” Stress test Crisis preparedness has turned into a political issue in France as record-breaking heat and wildfires are forcing the country to reckon with its ability to respond to emergencies. Advertisement Advertisement Last summer, the government updated the country’s National Resilience Strategy, a roadmap on how to “maintain the functions essential to collective life” in the face of war or natural disasters. Since the start of the summer, many French regions have faced unprecedented temperatures, with mercury levels setting multiple records in June. In the country’s southwest, out-of-control wildfires fueled by extreme heat and drought forced mass evacuations that affected more than 200,000 people. In Paris, the mayor made a desperate plea to large-scale food retailers to mobilize ice stocks over fears that first responders would run out of much-needed cubes to cool down victims of heatstroke. Opposition parties were quick to attack the government over what they described as a widespread lack of preparedness, forcing the executive to defend itself. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also announced that the government would submit a bill to parliament to improve emergency response systems. “We want to refocus fire and rescue services on their core mission and adapt our organization to the crises that lie ahead,” said Lecornu Sunday in an interview with La Tribune Dimanche . https://bnn-news.com/likely-location-of-.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home Baltics Latvia Latvia Social Likely location of missing Latvians at time of Himalayan disaster identified LETA September 9, 2026 Facebook Twitter Photo: Mike M/Pexels Chinese authorities have officially confirmed that all 33 missing Latvian nationals had been in China and have no information indicating that the travellers crossed the border back into Nepal, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told LETA. According to the MFA, this means that the Latvian nationals were most likely on the Tibetan side of the Himalayas when the catastrophic floods and mudslides struck. Chinese authorities have also asked Latvia to provide DNA samples for comparison. It was previously reported that belongings belonging to the travellers had been found on the Chinese side near the border crossing. The MFA is currently determining whether the items will be photographed and whether the images will be made available for identification. Meanwhile, Red Cross DNA experts are expected to arrive in Nepal this week to speed up and facilitate the comparison of samples. MFA Consular Department representative Jurģis Barkāns, who is currently in Nepal, is also exploring options for transporting to Latvia the travellers’ belongings left behind at hotels. The MFA noted that the amount of belongings must first be established and it must be determined whether the items can be identified. Arrangements could then be made with transport companies to bring them to Latvia. The MFA stressed that not all relatives have received or fully understood the information sent last week regarding the necessary steps and formalities. Relatives have been sent a detailed explanation compiling information from the Ministry of Welfare, Ministry of Justice, Latvian Association of Local and Regional Governments, and Ministry of Education and Science. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Justice will hold a meeting with relatives to explain the information provided and answer their questions. The MFA is also asking relatives who are not currently on the ministry’s contact list but believe they should receive information directly to get in touch. The ministry stressed that it is currently important for all relatives to obtain a certificate confirming the travellers’ status as missing persons. The Latvian nationals have been placed on an international missing persons list, and relatives need the relevant certificate to complete other formalities. The Chancery of the President of Latvia has also asked the MFA to contact the Ombudsman, who is prepared, where possible, to advise both the ministry and the relatives of the missing people. Information about this option has been sent to the relatives. As previously reported, the collapse of a glacier on the 26th of August triggered a flow of ice debris, causing water and mud to surge from a glacial lake and resulting in widespread destruction in Nepal and China. As of the 3rd of September, the confirmed death toll had reached 1,252, while another 4,216 people were considered missing. A large group of Latvian tourists organised by yoga enthusiasts from Yantra was also near the epicentre of the disaster, while a smaller number of Latvian tourists were in the disaster zone as part of a group organised by the local company Mighty Himalayan Trek. The MFA is aware that three Latvian residents who were in the region at the time were not affected by the flood-triggered mudslide in Nepal, while 33 are currently considered missing. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr3e.text: Image source, MSF via Reuters Image caption, Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town has been treating people wounded in Monday's attack on the market By Richard Kagoe ,Â Lucy Fleming Â and Â Richard Irvine-Brown ,Â BBC Verify Published 20 October 2026, 15:24 BST Updated 5 minutes ago Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral. The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said. A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF. The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011. South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Published 13 November 2025 Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line Published 25 February Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict. The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes. "We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson StÃ©phane Dujarric said on Monday , external . The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said. Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands. The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state. A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said. Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said. Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known. Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them. The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border. On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people. "It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying. BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks. It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market. Image source, TikTok screengrab Image caption, This screengrab is from a video taken 600m from Amiet Market Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. On Monday, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town. "So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement. Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source. It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport. Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.
